title: Memory & Skew Recognition Track — Senior
description: A 10-exercise senior recognition track at GridUnion Continental scale (850M meters, 8TB+ across 6 teams, 4 countries, 30 regions). Read multi-team executor sizing audits, fetch-failure cascades, off-heap memory breakdowns, JVM-tuning that made it worse, dynamic-allocation thrash, capacity contracts, and 50–80 line architectural pipelines. Five modules: PMSS1 Executor Sizing · PMSS2 Fetch Failures · PMSS3 Off-Heap and JVM · PMSS4 Multi-Team Architecture · PMSS5 Architectural Pipelines. Companion to PSS6 + PSS9; chains PMSI3.2 + PMSI4.2.

datasets.description: Schema reference (sample rows). Senior scenarios describe GridUnion Continental at platform scale (850M meters across 4 countries, 30 regions, 6 teams, 8TB+ archive); the CSV itself is a small sample for schema reference.
Substations reference. Anchors multi-team architectural scenarios.

tasks.title: The Executor Sizing That Six Teams Disagree On

description.context: GridUnion Continental shares one cluster across 6 teams. Each team independently chose executor sizes for their own workload. Last quarter the cluster's tail-latency SLA started missing for 4 of the 6 teams, even though no team's individual pipeline regressed. The Platform team has audit data showing each team's chosen executor size and a 23% container fragmentation pattern. As architect, identify which team's choice imposes the highest cross-team cost.
description.task: Which team's sizing choice imposes the highest cross-team cost, and what is the resolution?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Cluster Total: 96 nodes × 64g RAM × 16 cores

Fragmentation: 23% of node capacity unschedulable as 4-8g chunks

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Six-team executor sizing audit; identify the architecturally-disruptive choice across competing workloads

evidence.label: Architecture artifact
evidence.content:
# Cluster sizing audit — six teams sharing 96 nodes × 64g RAM × 16 cores

Team A (Billing):    8 execs × 4g × 2 cores       (256 cores total, 32g RAM)
Team B (Reporting): 32 execs × 8g × 4 cores       (128 cores, 256g)
Team C (Risk):       16 execs × 16g × 8 cores      (128 cores, 256g)
Team D (ML):          4 execs × 32g × 16 cores     (64 cores, 128g)
Team E (Audit):       2 execs × 64g × 16 cores     (32 cores, 128g)  ← single-node containers
Team F (Ops):       32 execs × 8g × 4 cores       (128 cores, 256g)

# Symptoms (last quarter)
# - Teams A, B, C, F missing tail-latency SLA
# - Teams D, E hitting their own SLAs comfortably
# - Cluster utilization at 78% (room to spare)
# - Container fragmentation: 23% of node capacity unschedulable as 4-8g chunks

fields.label: Which team's sizing choice imposes the highest cross-team cost, and what is the resolution?
options: Team A — too small. Many tiny executors create scheduling overhead and fragment shuffle blocks across many writers. Migrate Team A to 16g × 8-core executors aligned with the cluster median.

Team E — single-node containers consume entire nodes. Other teams' 4-8g requests cannot fit on those 2 nodes. The 23% fragmentation traces to this monopoly. Fix: max-executor-size 32g; Team E runs 4 × 32g.
Team D — full-core executors. The 16-core sizing saturates node CPU, leaving other teams competing for compute even when memory is available. Drop Team D to 8 cores per executor.
Teams B and F — duplicate sizing pattern. Together they consume 256g and 256 cores in identical executors, exhausting medium-tier slots. One team adopts a different sizing tier.
fields.correctAnswer: Team E — single-node containers consume entire nodes. Other teams' 4-8g requests cannot fit on those 2 nodes. The 23% fragmentation traces to this monopoly. Fix: max-executor-size 32g; Team E runs 4 × 32g.
fields.rationale: Team E's 64g/16-core executors map 1:1 to physical nodes. When Team E occupies node N, no other team can place ANY executor there. The 23% fragmentation is the smoking gun: small executor requests cannot fit on Team E's nodes. Team E externalizes the cost while hitting its own SLA. Fix: Platform-side max-executor-size policy; Team E runs 4×32g instead of 2×64g — same total, no monopoly.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Many-small is a victim of node monopolization, not the cause of fragmentation.

Option C: Real-but-secondary CPU concern; 32g containers DO leave room for smaller executors on the same node.

Option D: Identical sizing across teams is fair competition, not architectural inequity.

tasks.pssReference: PSS1 lesson 4 (Multi-Tenant Cluster Architecture), PSS6 lesson 7 (Executor Sizing as Cross-Team Decision).

tasks.title: Two Sizing Configs, Same Workload — Which Wins?

description.context: GridUnion's Risk team runs the same nightly portfolio-risk pipeline with two different executor sizing configurations on isolated cluster slices. Both use the same total cluster resource (256 cores, 1024g RAM). Config A: 64 executors × 4 cores × 16g. Config B: 16 executors × 16 cores × 64g. The pipeline does an 850M-row sort-merge join, a 12-hop chain of medium-cardinality groupBys, and a final aggregation.
description.task: Which config wins for this workload, and what is the structural reason?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Config A: 64 executors × 4 cores × 16g (small)

Config B: 16 executors × 16 cores × 64g (large)

Shuffle Partitions: 800

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Same workload, two sizing configurations; senior reasoning about parallelism, memory headroom, and shuffle fan-out simultaneously

evidence.label: Config A — many small
evidence.content:
Total: 64 × (4 cores × 16g) = 256 cores, 1024g

Pros:
- Smaller GC pause per executor (16g heap)
- Failed-executor blast radius 1/64

Cons:
- More shuffle fan-out (each partition × 64 readers)
- ~5g per task slot (16g / 4 cores - JVM overhead)
- More executor-to-executor traffic during shuffle reads

evidence.label: Config B — few large
evidence.content:
Total: 16 × (16 cores × 64g) = 256 cores, 1024g

Pros:
- ~16g per task slot
- Within-node task communication (no network)
- Larger broadcast cache (one broadcast, 16 cores)
- Fewer shuffle fan-out targets (16 readers)

Cons:
- 64g heap risks longer GC pauses
- Failed-executor blast radius 1/16
- Single-node container risk (PMSS1.1)

fields.label: Which config wins for this workload, and what is the structural reason?
options: Config A — both have 256 task slots, but A's smaller 16g heaps win on GC P99. The chain's per-task wall-clock is dominated by GC. Many-small is the structural choice for any workload.

Config B. The shuffle is heavy (850M rows × 800 partitions). A's 64 readers per partition fragment data into 64 small reads with high overhead; B's 16 readers produce larger payloads. Shuffle-heavy workloads scale with reader count.

Both equivalent because parallelism is governed by spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (800 in both) and total CPU is identical. The choice is a tuning detail; pick whichever the team is more comfortable with.

Config A — 64 smaller executors give Spark's dynamic allocation more granularity. When the cluster has spare capacity, A can request a few more 16g executors easily; B's 64g granularity makes scaling hard.
fields.correctAnswer: Config B. The shuffle is heavy (850M rows × 800 partitions). A's 64 readers per partition fragment data into 64 small reads with high overhead; B's 16 readers produce larger payloads. Shuffle-heavy workloads scale with reader count.
fields.rationale: Shuffle fan-out distinguishes the two configs. Each shuffle partition's data is read by every executor with downstream tasks on that partition. A's 64 executors fragment the read into 64 small payloads per partition; B's 16 executors get larger reads. Network throughput depends on payload size: 64 small reads cost more total time than 16 large ones. Across 800 partitions and a 12-hop chain, the difference accumulates to 2-3× shuffle phase. Shuffle-heavy workloads scale with reader count, not core count.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Confuses task slots with executor count. Both have 256 slots; the difference is reader count for shuffle.

Option C: Dismisses sizing as tuning. Shuffle fan-out is structural, not tunable.

Option D: Picks dynamic allocation granularity; secondary to shuffle network cost.

tasks.pssReference: PSS6 lessons 7-8 (Executor Sizing for Shuffle-Heavy Workloads), PSS6 lesson 9 (Reader Count vs Task Count).

tasks.title: Reading a Fetch-Failure Cascade in the UI

description.context: GridUnion's Risk team's nightly pipeline failed at 02:47 with the cluster's worst kind of error: a fetch-failure cascade. The Spark UI shows three retried stages and a long executor-log trail. The on-call senior engineer asks the team to read the cascade pattern carefully — which failure was the ROOT CAUSE and which were the cascade.
description.task: What is the ROOT CAUSE of the cascade, and what would have prevented it?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
External Shuffle Service: NOT enabled

Executor Count: 16

Stage Retried: Stage 12 (sort-merge join), 3 retries

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Spark UI Stages page + executor log excerpt showing a fetch-failure cascade across multiple retries

evidence.label: Snapshot
evidence.content:
Spark UI — Stages page (failed pipeline)

Stage 12 — sort-merge join (12M × 8M rows)
  Attempt 1: failed (3 tasks failed with FetchFailedException)
  Attempt 2: failed (5 tasks failed with FetchFailedException)
  Attempt 3: failed (8 tasks failed; stage aborted; pipeline failed)

Executor log timeline:
02:31:14  ExecutorLost: executor-7 (heartbeat timeout, container exit code 143)
02:32:02  TaskSetManager: FetchFailedException on executor-1
            (could not fetch shuffle block from executor-7:10000)
02:32:18  TaskSetManager: FetchFailedException on executor-4
            (could not fetch shuffle block from executor-7:10000)
02:33:01  Stage 12 retry started (attempt 2)
02:35:42  ExecutorLost: executor-9 (OOM, container kill)
02:36:18  FetchFailedException on executor-12 (executor-9:10000)
02:38:14  Stage 12 retry started (attempt 3)
02:42:01  ExecutorLost: executor-3 (OOM, container kill)
02:47:00  Stage 12 aborted; pipeline failed

Cluster config:
  spark.shuffle.service.enabled = false  (default for this cluster)
  spark.network.timeout = 120s

fields.label: What is the ROOT CAUSE of the cascade, and what would have prevented it?
options: FetchFailedException on executor-1 at 02:32:02 — the network blip caused the first failure, triggering retries that cascaded into OOMs. Fix: raise spark.network.timeout to 300s so transient blips do not register as fetch failures.

OOMs on executors 9 and 3 at 02:35 and 02:42 — those are why the retried stages failed. The first executor lost at 02:31 was unrelated (heartbeat timeout). Fix: raise --executor-memory to prevent the OOMs.

Executor-7's loss at 02:31:14 — the FIRST failure (exit code 143). When executor-7 died, its shuffle output became unreachable; downstream tasks failed with FetchFailedException. Retries piled work onto survivors. Fix: enable spark.shuffle.service.enabled.

The 3-retry policy itself — Spark's default of 4 retries gave the cascade 3 chances to compound. With max-retries=1, the pipeline would have failed at attempt 1 with a clean error. Fix: set spark.task.maxFailures=1.
fields.correctAnswer: Executor-7's loss at 02:31:14 — the FIRST failure (exit code 143). When executor-7 died, its shuffle output became unreachable; downstream tasks failed with FetchFailedException. Retries piled work onto survivors. Fix: enable spark.shuffle.service.enabled.
fields.rationale: Cascade root-cause analysis traces back to the earliest failure event in the timeline. When executor-7 died, its shuffle output on local disk became unreachable. Downstream FetchFailedException on executors 1 and 4 are SYMPTOMS of executor-7's prior death. Retries doubled survivors' workload, OOMing executors 9 and 3. The architectural fix is the external shuffle service: shuffle output stored separately from executors survives executor death.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: FetchFailedException is a downstream consequence; ExecutorLost is the upstream cause.

Option B: Skips the first failure entirely. Cascade root-cause must trace to the EARLIEST event.

Option D: Retry policy is amplifier, not cause. Reducing retries makes failure faster but leaves the architectural single-point-of-failure.

tasks.pssReference: PSS6 lessons 4-5 (Shuffle Service and Fetch-Failure Recovery), PSS6 lesson 6 (External Shuffle Service Architecture).

tasks.title: The Stage Retried Three Times — Whose Fault?

description.context: GridUnion's Risk team's pipeline retried Stage 12 three times across three nights — Monday, Wednesday, Friday last week. Each night a different node hosted the failure. Initial analysis blamed bad disks. The Platform team's audit reveals: failed nodes were always the most CPU-saturated at the moment of failure, traced to scheduling decisions about which team's pipelines were running concurrently with Risk.
description.task: What is the diagnosis, whose responsibility is the fix, and why is 'fix the disks' wrong?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Common Pattern: Risk pipeline 02:00-04:00 overlaps Team B (01:30-04:00) and Team F (02:30-03:30)

External Shuffle Service: Enabled (the PMSS2.1 fix is in place)

Scheduler: fair-share, no per-team CPU quotas

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Cross-night Stage 12 retry analysis showing CPU saturation pattern, not hardware failure pattern

evidence.label: Architecture artifact
evidence.content:
# Stage 12 retry incident analysis (last week, three nights)

Monday    node-22 failed 02:34  CPU 94% (Team B Reporting on same node 02:26-02:34)
Wednesday node-44 failed 02:51  CPU 91% (Team F Ops on same node 02:45-02:51)
Friday    node-58 failed 03:12  CPU 96% (Team B Reporting on same node 03:04-03:12)

# Cluster scheduling policy: fair-share, no per-team CPU quotas
# External shuffle service: enabled (so individual executor death is recoverable)
# Risk team's pipeline: 12 executors × 8 cores × 32g; SLA 06:00
# Initial root-cause analysis: 'bad disks on failed nodes'
# Audit finding: failed disks tested healthy on Saturday; failure pattern is CPU saturation, not disk

fields.label: What is the diagnosis, whose responsibility is the fix, and why is 'fix the disks' wrong?
options: Cluster scheduler allows CPU oversubscription. Three teams saturate CPU; under saturation, JVM heartbeats time out, the driver registers ExecutorLost. Fix: Platform adds per-team CPU quotas. 'Disks' is wrong — they tested healthy.

Risk's executor sizing (12 × 8 cores × 32g) is too greedy; 8-core executors saturate node CPU when other teams' executors also need CPU on the same nodes. Responsibility: Risk drops to 4-core executors. 'Disks' is wrong — the symptom is CPU contention.

Team B's Reporting batch is misbehaving — it appears in 2 of 3 failures with high CPU bursts. Responsibility: Team B reduces CPU usage during the overlap window. 'Disks' is wrong; the symptom is contention from Team B.

Risk's 02:00 start conflicts with Team B (01:30-04:00) and Team F (02:30-03:30). Responsibility: Risk reschedules to 04:30 to avoid both windows. 'Disks' is wrong because the symptom is timing conflict.
fields.correctAnswer: Cluster scheduler allows CPU oversubscription. Three teams saturate CPU; under saturation, JVM heartbeats time out, the driver registers ExecutorLost. Fix: Platform adds per-team CPU quotas. 'Disks' is wrong — they tested healthy.
fields.rationale: Fair-share scheduling without CPU quotas allows oversubscription. When 3 teams' threads contend on a node, all run slower. Spark's heartbeat thread misses its 120s window under sustained saturation; the driver registers ExecutorLost (heartbeat timeout) and retries. No individual team is misconfigured — the COMBINATION without quotas produces the inequity. Fix is platform-side via cgroups CPU limits or YARN node-local constraints. The disk hypothesis came from misreading ExecutorLost as hardware failure.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Blames Risk sizing. 8-core sizing is reasonable in isolation; the inequity is at the policy level.

Option C: Blames Team B. Team B is correctly sized; only the COMBINATION without quotas produces the problem.

Option D: Shifts cost to Risk via reschedule. Rescheduling moves the conflict, does not eliminate the policy gap.

tasks.pssReference: PSS6 lesson 5 (Heartbeat Timeout and Cluster Scheduling), PSS9 lesson 7 (Architectural Choice and Multi-Team Cost Attribution).

tasks.title: Reading the Off-Heap Memory Footprint

description.context: GridUnion's Risk team's senior engineer is reviewing an executor that has 8GB heap configured but shows 12GB resident set size (RSS) in the OS-level audit. The container budget is 14GB. The Platform team asks: where is the missing 4GB, and is the executor in danger of being killed?
description.task: Which region accounts for the largest portion of the 4GB delta, and is the executor at risk?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Executor Memory: 8GB heap

Executor Memoryoverhead: 6GB

Container Total: 14GB

Rss Measured: 12GB

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Executor RSS breakdown: heap 8GB, RSS 12GB, container budget 14GB; account for the off-heap regions

evidence.label: Snapshot
evidence.content:
Executor process memory breakdown (audit at 02:14, mid-pipeline)

Region                              Size       Notes
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
JVM heap (committed)                 7.8 GB    Spark managed (Tungsten + storage)
JVM metaspace + code cache           0.3 GB    JIT compilation artifacts
JVM thread stacks (44 threads)       0.04 GB   Spark task threads + driver RPC
Netty direct buffers                 1.2 GB    Shuffle network I/O
Tungsten off-heap (UnsafeRow)        1.8 GB    spark.memory.offHeap.enabled=true
Broadcast cache (off-heap)           0.5 GB    Persistent broadcast variables
Native library allocations            0.1 GB    libsnappy, libsasl, etc.
Python interpreter (this exec)       0.0 GB    No PySpark UDFs in this pipeline
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Total RSS                           ~12.0 GB

fields.label: Which region accounts for the largest portion of the 4GB delta, and is the executor at risk?
options: JVM metaspace and code cache (0.3 GB) plus thread stacks — JVM internals that grow as the application runs longer. At risk because metaspace grows unbounded; fix: -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m.

Tungsten off-heap (1.8 GB) driven by spark.memory.offHeap.enabled. Combined with Netty's 1.2 GB and broadcast cache 0.5 GB, off-heap accounts for ~3.5 GB of the 4 GB delta. 2 GB headroom — moderate risk under shuffle peaks.
The heap itself at 7.8 GB; other regions sum to ~4 GB but no single region dominates. At risk because heap is at 97.5% of its 8 GB configured limit. Fix: raise --executor-memory to 12 GB.
The broadcast cache at 0.5 GB; broadcast variables persist across stages and accumulate. At risk because broadcast cache is unbounded; fix: call sc.broadcast().destroy() between stages.
fields.correctAnswer: Tungsten off-heap (1.8 GB) driven by spark.memory.offHeap.enabled. Combined with Netty's 1.2 GB and broadcast cache 0.5 GB, off-heap accounts for ~3.5 GB of the 4 GB delta. 2 GB headroom — moderate risk under shuffle peaks.
fields.rationale: Heap is 7.8 GB; everything else sums to 4 GB. Within that, Tungsten off-heap (1.8 GB) is the largest single region, followed by Netty direct buffers (1.2 GB) and broadcast cache (0.5 GB). These are the senior-level 'invisible' memory consumers — they don't appear in heap dumps or GC logs, but DO appear in OS-level RSS that drives container-kill decisions. With 2 GB headroom against the 14 GB budget, a large skewed shuffle could push Netty to 2.5+ GB and consume the headroom.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks JVM metaspace as dominant. Metaspace is small (0.3 GB) compared to Tungsten (1.8 GB).

Option C: Confuses heap-vs-configured with heap-vs-budget. Container budget is 14 GB, not 8 GB.

Option D: Picks broadcast cache. 0.5 GB is real but smaller than Tungsten or Netty.

tasks.pssReference: PSS6 lessons 2-3 (Off-Heap Memory Architecture), PSS6 lesson 8 (Tungsten and Netty Direct Buffer Accounting).

tasks.title: G1GC Tuning That Made It Worse

description.context: GridUnion's ML team's senior engineer noticed long G1GC pauses (12-15 seconds) on their 64 GB executors. They tuned G1GC by raising G1HeapRegionSize from the default 32MB to 128MB, hoping fewer/larger regions would reduce GC overhead. The pauses got WORSE — now 25-30 seconds, and a new failure mode appeared: long full-heap collections that the previous setup never triggered.
description.task: Why did raising G1HeapRegionSize make GC worse, and what other setting needed to change with it?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Executor Memory: 64g

Original Gc Pause P99: 12-15s

New Gc Pause P99: 25-30s

Tuning Change: G1HeapRegionSize 32m → 128m (IHOP=45% unchanged)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: G1GC tuning that introduced full-heap collection pathology by raising G1HeapRegionSize without raising InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent

evidence.label: Snapshot
evidence.content:
# Original config
--executor-memory 64g
# (default G1GC: G1HeapRegionSize=32MB, IHOP=45%)

# Observed:
#   - Average GC pause 12-15s
#   - No full-heap collections
#   - Throughput acceptable but pause-sensitive jobs missed SLA

# Engineer's tuning change
--executor-memory 64g
--conf 'spark.executor.extraJavaOptions=-XX:+UseG1GC -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=128m'
# (default IHOP=45% unchanged)

# New observation:
#   - Average GC pause 25-30s (worse)
#   - Occasional full-heap collection (multi-minute STW)
#   - Some tasks fail with executor heartbeat timeout during the full collection

# Question: what additional setting needed to be tuned alongside G1HeapRegionSize?

fields.label: Why did raising G1HeapRegionSize make GC worse, and what other setting needed to change with it?
options: Larger regions need higher InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent (IHOP). Default IHOP=45% triggers concurrent GC by occupancy. With 128MB regions on 64GB, by IHOP trigger more old-gen accumulated than the cycle can clear; falls back to full-heap. Fix: raise IHOP to ~60-70.

Larger regions create 'humongous' allocations: objects > 50% region size go directly to old gen. Medium shuffle buffers (16-64MB) qualify and accumulate, eventually triggering full-heap collections. Fix: keep G1HeapRegionSize default.

Larger regions reduce the count from ~2000 to ~500; G1's mixed-collection efficiency degrades because each cycle reclaims a smaller fraction. Fix: also raise spark.executor.cores from 8 to 16 to keep CPU saturated during GC cycles.

G1HeapRegionSize=128MB is incompatible with executor heaps over 32GB; G1GC's region tracking grows non-linearly past that threshold. Fix: switch from G1GC to ZGC for heaps over 32GB; ZGC pauses are sub-millisecond.
fields.correctAnswer: Larger regions need higher InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent (IHOP). Default IHOP=45% triggers concurrent GC by occupancy. With 128MB regions on 64GB, by IHOP trigger more old-gen accumulated than the cycle can clear; falls back to full-heap. Fix: raise IHOP to ~60-70.
fields.rationale: G1GC's behavior depends on the relationship between region size and IHOP. With 32MB regions on 64GB heap (~2000 regions), concurrent cycles run frequently enough to keep up with allocation. Raising regions to 128MB (~500 regions) makes each region 4× denser; concurrent marking takes longer per region. By the time IHOP fires at 45%, allocation has outpaced concurrent progress; G1 falls back to a FULL HEAP collection (multi-minute STW). Raising IHOP to 60-70 starts the cycle earlier in absolute terms. This is paired tuning — neither setting works in isolation.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Identifies a real concern (humongous allocations) but it produces accelerated old-gen growth, not full-heap fallback alone.

Option C: Invents a mixed-collection efficiency interaction with executor cores; cores setting is unrelated.

Option D: Invents a 32GB cliff for G1HeapRegionSize that does not exist.

tasks.pssReference: PSS6 lesson 9 (G1GC Tuning), PSS6 lesson 10 (Coupled Parameters in JVM Tuning).

tasks.title: Dynamic Allocation Thrash Across Three Teams

description.context: Three teams at GridUnion enabled dynamic allocation independently. Team A set min=4, max=64. Team B min=20, max=40. Team C min=8, max=128. Cluster total capacity 200 executors. Sustained thrash: every 90 seconds the cluster oscillates — executor counts ramp up, then are reclaimed, then ramp again. CPU never settles. None of the teams' settings looks pathological in isolation.
description.task: Which team's setting drives the thrash, and what is the unified policy fix?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Team A: min=4, max=64

Team B: min=20, max=40

Team C: min=8, max=128

Total Max Requested: 232 executors (capacity 200; 16% over)

Thrash Period: 90 seconds

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Three teams' independent dynamic-allocation settings interacting on a shared cluster, producing 90-second oscillation

evidence.label: Architecture artifact
evidence.content:
# Three teams, three independent dynamic-allocation settings

Team A: min=4   max=64   idleTimeout=60s   (bursty; idle 70% of day)
Team B: min=20  max=40   idleTimeout=60s   (steady)
Team C: min=8   max=128  idleTimeout=60s   (very bursty: spikes 100+, idle 90%)

Cluster capacity: 200 executors
Sum of max: 64 + 40 + 128 = 232 (16% over capacity)

# Observed thrash pattern
T+0s    Team C spikes to 100; pulls executors from A and B's idle pool
T+5s    Team A spikes to 30; pulls from B and C
T+30s   Both A and C idle; idleTimeout begins counting
T+90s   A and C release executors; cluster looks 'settled' briefly
T+95s   Team C spikes again; cycle restarts

# CPU oscillates 40-85%, never settles to a steady state

fields.label: Which team's setting drives the thrash, and what is the unified policy fix?
options: Team A — min=4 too low. When A drops to 4, the next request must spin up new executors from cold, contributing to the oscillation. Fix: Team A raises min to 16 to maintain warm capacity.
Team B — min=20 holds 20 executors permanently, leaving only 180 of true elastic capacity for the others. When A and C burst, they compete for the smaller pool. Fix: Team B drops min to 8.

Team C — max=128 pulls half the cluster in one burst. Combined with A's burst, demand exceeds 200 and forces premature reclamation. Underlying issue: sum-of-max (232 > 200) is allowed. Fix: Platform enforces sum-of-max ≤ capacity.

All three teams' default idleTimeout=60s — reclamation has a fixed 60s lag. The 90-second period is 60s idle + 30s ramp. Fix: each team raises idleTimeout to 300s so executors stay warm longer between bursts.
fields.correctAnswer: Team C — max=128 pulls half the cluster in one burst. Combined with A's burst, demand exceeds 200 and forces premature reclamation. Underlying issue: sum-of-max (232 > 200) is allowed. Fix: Platform enforces sum-of-max ≤ capacity.
fields.rationale: Overcommitted resource limits at the policy level produce instability that no individual team can resolve. With 232 max and 200 capacity, overlapping bursts force premature reclamation and the cycle repeats. Team C is the immediate trigger because their max=128 is the largest fraction, but the FAULT is the policy gap — Team C's max is correct in isolation. Fix is Platform-side: queue-style quotas or weighted-fair-share with max as advisory.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Blames Team A's min. min affects steady-state warm capacity, not burst dynamics.

Option B: Blames Team B. Team B's setting is reasonable in isolation.

Option D: Treats idleTimeout as cause. Timeout amplifies the period but does not produce overcommit.

tasks.pssReference: PSS6 lesson 11 (Dynamic Allocation Architecture), PSS9 lesson 7 (Multi-Team Resource Policy).

tasks.title: The Capacity Contract Without an Off-Heap Clause

description.context: GridUnion's Platform team and Risk team negotiated a capacity contract last quarter: Risk gets 16 executors at 32g heap each, totaling 512g of guaranteed memory. The contract was fulfilled and Risk's pipelines ran fine for two months. Last week Risk's pipeline started causing CLUSTER-WIDE OOMs — not Risk's own executors, but other teams' on shared nodes. Risk's heap is at 28g (within contract) but RSS at 56g — almost 2× the heap.
description.task: What is the architectural failure mode, and whose responsibility is the fix?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Contract Heap Per Executor: 32g

Actual Rss Per Executor: 56g (24g over heap, unbudgeted)

Recent Change: Risk added Python UDF using native ML library 6 weeks ago

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Capacity contract specifying heap-only memory; Risk's UDF native library blew through unbudgeted off-heap and impacted other teams

evidence.label: Architecture artifact
evidence.content:
# Capacity contract — Risk team

## Original contract (Q2 2025)
  16 executors × 32g heap = 512g guaranteed memory
  Off-heap allocation: not specified
  Container budget per executor: not specified

## Audit measurements (last week, mid-pipeline)
  Heap usage:           28g per executor (within 32g contract ✓)
  RSS:                  56g per executor (24g over heap, unbudgeted off-heap)
  Container RSS total:  896g (75% over the 512g 'agreed' total)

## Recent change (6 weeks ago)
  Risk added a Python UDF using a native ML library (PyTorch CPU inference)
  The native library allocates ~22g per worker process for model weights

## Cluster impact
  Other teams' executors on shared nodes failing with container kills
  Affected teams: A (Billing), F (Ops), B (Reporting)
  Risk team's own pipeline runs fine (their executors hit RSS budget but not heap OOM)

fields.label: What is the architectural failure mode, and whose responsibility is the fix?
options: Risk is at fault — they added a 22g native library without informing Platform of the off-heap impact. Fix: Risk reverts the native library or migrates to a JVM-native ML implementation that respects the heap-only contract.

The contract is at fault — it specified heap but did not specify off-heap or container budget. Risk is contractually compliant on heap (28g of 32g). Fix is Platform-side: revise contract to specify total container budget or use cgroups RSS limits.

The cluster is at fault — Spark's container manager should detect when an executor's RSS exceeds heap by more than 50% and proactively kill that executor before impacting others. Fix: enable spark.executor.processTreeMetrics.enabled and add a watchdog over budget.

Other teams are at fault — they should have requested explicit nodes for their workloads via node-affinity rules, not shared nodes with Risk. Fix: A, F, B each request dedicated-node allocations; Risk continues on shared nodes.
fields.correctAnswer: The contract is at fault — it specified heap but did not specify off-heap or container budget. Risk is contractually compliant on heap (28g of 32g). Fix is Platform-side: revise contract to specify total container budget or use cgroups RSS limits.
fields.rationale: Missing-clause contracts produce architectural failure modes when teams add legitimate but unspecified workloads. The contract did not specify off-heap, so Risk's 22g native library is technically not a violation. The failure is INCOMPLETE CONTRACT — it specified one dimension (heap) when the cluster budgets a different dimension (total RSS). Holding teams to unspecified terms is non-scalable. Fix is Platform-side: contracts must specify the resource the SHARED SYSTEM allocates (total RSS), enforced via cgroups.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Blames Risk for following the explicit contract. Holding teams to unspecified terms is non-scalable.

Option C: Externalizes responsibility to tooling. Tooling enforces; contract design is the policy decision.

Option D: Blames affected teams. Node-affinity is a workaround, not a fix for the systemic policy gap.

tasks.pssReference: PSS9 lesson 7 (Multi-Team Capacity Contracts), PSS6 lesson 12 (Off-Heap Accounting in Shared Clusters).

tasks.title: Multi-Team Memory Audit Across Three Pipelines

description.context: GridUnion's three teams share an executor pool during the 02:00-04:00 batch window. Risk runs portfolio revaluation; Reporting runs daily aggregation; Ops runs compaction. The Platform team conducted a memory audit across all three pipelines simultaneously. Read the multi-pipeline snapshot and answer four targeted questions about the cross-team memory dynamics.
description.task: Read the artifact above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Three concurrent pipelines' memory profiles audited at the same instant; cross-team interaction questions

evidence.label: Architecture artifact
evidence.content:
# Concurrent memory audit — three teams, 02:14:33 timestamp

## Risk team — portfolio revaluation
  16 executors × 32g heap × 8 cores  (contract: 512g heap)
  Heap usage:    24g per exec  (75%)  — within contract
  RSS:           54g per exec         — 22g over heap (off-heap from PyTorch UDF)
  Broadcast cache: 4.2g per exec       — large reference-data broadcast
  Stage:         sort-merge join (12B rows)

## Reporting team — daily aggregation
  32 executors × 16g heap × 4 cores  (contract: 512g heap)
  Heap usage:    14g per exec (87%)  — near contract limit
  RSS:           18g per exec         — 4g over (Netty buffers + JVM internals)
  Broadcast cache: 0.8g per exec
  Stage:         3-hop chain of medium-cardinality groupBys

## Ops team — daily compaction
  Dynamic allocation: min=4, max=24, currently 18 executors
  16g heap × 4 cores per exec
  Heap usage:    11g per exec (69%)
  RSS:           14g per exec
  Broadcast cache: 0.2g per exec
  Stage:         file-level compaction (re-write small Parquet files into larger ones)

## Cluster total at this instant
  Total RSS across three teams: 16×54 + 32×18 + 18×14 = 864 + 576 + 252 = 1692g
  Cluster capacity: 1800g  (108g headroom = 6%)
  YARN/cgroups: shared-pool (no per-team RSS quotas)
  External shuffle service: enabled

## Recent incidents (last 7 days)
  - Reporting executors hit container kills 3 times when Risk's stage spikes
  - Ops scaled up to 24 (max) during Risk peak; was reclaimed by Risk's burst
  - Risk's own pipeline: no failures (their executors kill OTHER teams' executors first)

fields.label: Q1 — Risk's broadcast cache 4.2g × 16 = 67g. Reporting's 0.8g × 32 = 25g. Both teams broadcast independently. What architectural property produces the cross-team interaction?
options: Broadcasts on each executor compete with storage memory. Risk's 4.2g crowds out cached blocks. Cross-team interaction is at the NODE level: Risk's broadcasts crowd out Reporting's container budget on shared nodes.
Broadcasts are deduplicated cluster-wide via SparkSession sharing, so 67g + 25g = 92g actual usage, much less than the team-by-team sum suggests. Cross-team interaction is minimal.
Broadcasts are stored per-executor; the totals do NOT interact across teams. The cross-team interaction visible in the audit comes from heap and Tungsten regions, not broadcast.

Broadcasts are sent via Spark's RPC service; large broadcasts saturate RPC bandwidth shared across teams. Cross-team interaction is bandwidth contention. Fix: use disk-based shuffle service for broadcasts.
fields.correctAnswer: Broadcasts on each executor compete with storage memory. Risk's 4.2g crowds out cached blocks. Cross-team interaction is at the NODE level: Risk's broadcasts crowd out Reporting's container budget on shared nodes.
fields.rationale: Broadcasts are stored ON each executor (not deduplicated cluster-wide). The cross-team interaction emerges at the NODE level: when Risk's executor and Reporting's executor are co-located, the node's total memory budget is what the OS allocates. Risk's 4.2g broadcast contributes to RSS that competes with Reporting's RSS for total node capacity. Off-heap broadcast cache shows up in OS-level RSS that drives container-kill decisions.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents cluster-wide deduplication. Each SparkSession's broadcasts are independent.

Option C: Treats broadcast as having no cross-team effects. Co-location on shared nodes produces RSS competition.

Option D: Invents RPC-bandwidth interaction. Bandwidth is real but small compared to RSS competition.

fields.label: Q2 — Ops scaled up to 24 during Risk's peak then was reclaimed back to ~8. What architectural lesson does the reclamation pattern teach?
options: Dynamic allocation works as designed: Ops scaled up when capacity was available, scaled down when Risk needed it. The architectural lesson is no shared-cluster pathology; both teams got what they needed.

Dynamic allocation is fundamentally broken in shared clusters because lower-priority tenants claim resources higher-priority tenants will need. Lesson: disable dynamic allocation cluster-wide and use static allocation only for predictability.
Dynamic allocation works at executor level but produces cluster-wide thrash visible in the 90-second oscillation. Lesson: use static allocation with explicit per-team max settings ≤ 90% of capacity.

Dynamic allocation reclamation has hidden cost: Ops's work in flight on reclaimed executors was lost or re-run on survivors. Reclamation is NOT free — it costs the borrower's work, pessimal for non-checkpointed workloads.
fields.correctAnswer: Dynamic allocation reclamation has hidden cost: Ops's work in flight on reclaimed executors was lost or re-run on survivors. Reclamation is NOT free — it costs the borrower's work, pessimal for non-checkpointed workloads.
fields.rationale: Reclamation has hidden cost. When Ops scaled from 24 down to 8, work in flight on reclaimed executors is either lost (re-runs on survivors) or aborted. For stateless workloads (compaction is stateless), the cost is small. For stateful workloads (broadcast hash tables, cached intermediates), the cost is high. Mitigation: spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout or disable for stateful workloads.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats reclamation as free. The borrower pays in lost work.

Option B: Over-generalizes. Dynamic allocation works for stateless workloads.

Option C: Imports the PMSS4.1 thrash pattern; relevant but not the specific lesson about reclamation cost.

fields.label: Q3 — Risk RSS 54g per executor (22g over the 32g heap contract). Contract specified heap only. Reporting hits container kills when co-located. What is the responsibility-attribution outcome?
options: Compliant on the explicit terms (24g of 32g cap); off-heap was not specified in the agreement. No obligation exists to constrain the 22g native library. The other workload's container failures trace to a missing-clause issue owned by Platform.

Risk is responsible regardless of contract literalism — adding a 22g native library that affects shared infrastructure is a violation of good-neighbor norms. Risk should revert the library or migrate to JVM-native ML.

Fault is shared between Risk (for adding off-heap) and Reporting (for being on shared nodes). Both adjust — Risk caps off-heap usage, Reporting requests dedicated nodes via node-affinity. Cost is split between both teams.

Platform is solely responsible because they provisioned without per-node RSS isolation. Both Risk and Reporting are blameless tenants of a misdesigned platform. Resolution: Platform deploys cgroups-based RSS isolation as a hot-fix.
fields.correctAnswer: Compliant on the explicit terms (24g of 32g cap); off-heap was not specified in the agreement. No obligation exists to constrain the 22g native library. The other workload's container failures trace to a missing-clause issue owned by Platform.
fields.rationale: Under the literal contract, Risk is compliant: 24g heap is under 32g; off-heap not constrained. Holding Risk to unspecified terms is non-scalable — every team would have to anticipate every undocumented constraint. Platform owns the fix because contract design is platform-side. The fix is to specify total container budget, off-heap budget, or use cgroups RSS limits at the OS level.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Substitutes good-neighbor norms for explicit policy. Norms are non-scalable.

Option C: Splits responsibility ambiguously. Architectural fixes need clear ownership.

Option D: Picks a valid mechanism but misses the contract-design lesson.

fields.label: Q4 — Cluster total RSS is 1692g of 1800g (6% headroom). What is the senior-level architectural observation?
options: Cluster is dangerously over-utilized; 6% leaves no buffer for unexpected bursts. Architectural observation: the three teams collectively oversubscribe. Response: Platform expands capacity or reduces per-team allocations to 20-30% headroom.

Cluster is healthily utilized at 94% — capacity plans should maximize utilization. 6% headroom is appropriate for batch workloads where occasional kills are recoverable. No response needed at the architectural level.
The 6% averages across teams; per-team headroom is what matters. Risk has 0%, Reporting 25%, Ops 60%. Response: reallocate from Reporting/Ops to Risk to balance per-team headroom across the cluster.

The 6% is emergent: no team aimed for 94% utilization, but the COMBINATION produces it. Emergent over-utilization is the norm under permissive policies. Response: enforce policy invariants (sum-of-allocations ≤ capacity, RSS quotas).
fields.correctAnswer: The 6% is emergent: no team aimed for 94% utilization, but the COMBINATION produces it. Emergent over-utilization is the norm under permissive policies. Response: enforce policy invariants (sum-of-allocations ≤ capacity, RSS quotas).
fields.rationale: Aggregate state in shared clusters is the senior-architect's primary lever. Per-team correctness does not guarantee aggregate correctness. The proper response is to enforce policy invariants at the cluster level — sum-of-allocations ≤ capacity, per-team off-heap budgets, RSS quotas via cgroups. Policy invariants on aggregate state are the only scalable approach to multi-team capacity.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Frames response as capacity expansion. The fix is policy enforcement.

Option B: Treats 94% as desirable. Bursty workloads need lower steady-state utilization.

Option C: Suggests reallocation. Does not address unconstrained aggregate state.

tasks.pssReference: PSS9 lessons 7-9 (Multi-Team Cluster Architecture, Capacity Contracts, Emergent Cluster State).

tasks.title: The Pipeline With Five Senior-Level Architectural Memory Problems

description.context: Final exercise of the Senior track. A GridUnion pipeline runs nightly across the multi-team cluster. Every other week it triggers a cluster-wide incident: fetch failures, container kills on other teams' executors, dynamic-allocation thrash, and a salt-after-AQE cascade. Investigation traces the symptoms to five distinct Senior-level architectural memory-and-skew problems in the same 80-line pipeline.
description.task: Read the artifact above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 80-line cross-team pipeline with five Senior-level architectural memory problems

evidence.label: snippet.code
evidence.content:
# Risk team — portfolio reval pipeline (runs nightly 02:00-05:00)
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import (col, sum, broadcast, expr, lit,
                                     concat, split, hash, abs as f_abs)

spark = (SparkSession.builder
    .appName('risk-portfolio-reval')
    .config('spark.executor.memory', '32g')
    .config('spark.executor.memoryOverhead', '4g')
    .config('spark.executor.cores', '8')
    .config('spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled', 'true')
    .config('spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors', '4')
    .config('spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors', '128')
    .config('spark.shuffle.service.enabled', 'false')
    .config('spark.sql.adaptive.enabled', 'true')
    .config('spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled', 'true')
    .config('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', '400')
    .getOrCreate())

# Step 1: load 12B-row positions table
positions = spark.read.parquet('silver/positions/2026-04-30/')

# Step 2: salt for skew on counterparty_id (5 dominant counterparties)
#   Salt factor 10 (engineer's heuristic, not calculated from distribution)
salted_pos = positions.withColumn('counterparty_salted',
    concat(col('counterparty_id'), lit('_'),
           (expr('rand() * 10').cast('int'))))

# Step 3: load market data (8B rows, 1.2TB)
market_data = spark.read.parquet('reference/market_data_2026-04-30/')

# Step 4: outer-join to market_data (full outer for completeness)
revalued = salted_pos.join(market_data,
    on='instrument_id', how='full_outer')

# Step 5: PyTorch-based stress test scoring (Python UDF using native lib)
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType
import torch  # PyTorch with CPU inference, ~22GB native memory per worker

stress_model = torch.load('/models/stress_model.pt')

@udf(returnType=DoubleType())
def score_stress(position_value, market_factor):
    with torch.no_grad():
        return float(stress_model(
            torch.tensor([position_value, market_factor]).unsqueeze(0)
        ).item())

scored = revalued.withColumn('stress_score',
    score_stress(col('position_value'), col('market_factor')))

# Step 6: aggregate to per-counterparty stress totals
stress_summary = scored.groupBy('counterparty_id').agg(
    sum('stress_score').alias('total_stress'))

# Step 7: write
stress_summary.write.mode('overwrite').partitionBy('counterparty_id').parquet(
    'gold/risk-stress/2026-04-30/')

fields.label: Architectural Problem #1 — Lines 5-11 (the SparkSession config) combined with the platform-wide audit showing other teams' max settings. Risk's max=128 on 200-executor cluster shared with Reporting (max=40) and Ops (max=24). What is the architectural problem?
options: Sum-of-max (128+40+24=192) is just under capacity (200) and is therefore correctly bounded; this configuration is architecturally safe and there is no problem here to address.
Risk's max=128 is correct for their workload; the architectural problem is that the other two teams' max settings are too low to use the cluster fairly. Recommendation: raise other teams' max.

Sum-of-max (192) is set by individual teams without a Platform-enforced invariant. Current state happens to fit but the policy gap allows future overcommit. Fix: Platform-side invariant sum-of-max ≤ capacity.
Risk's max=128 is too aggressive; senior architects should set max conservatively at 50% of cluster capacity to leave room for unexpected bursts. Recommendation: drop Risk's max to 100.
fields.correctAnswer: Sum-of-max (192) is set by individual teams without a Platform-enforced invariant. Current state happens to fit but the policy gap allows future overcommit. Fix: Platform-side invariant sum-of-max ≤ capacity.
fields.rationale: PMSS4.1 covered overcommitted dynamic allocation. Current state (192 vs 200) fits, but the policy GAP allows future overcommit when any team raises their max. Senior architectural thinking is about INVARIANTS, not point-in-time state. Fix: Platform-side enforcement via queue-style quotas or weighted-fair-share with max as advisory.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats point-in-time state as safety. Senior thinking is about invariants.

Option B: Blames other teams' settings.

Option D: Picks an arbitrary cap.

fields.label: Architectural Problem #2 — Line 15 (`spark.shuffle.service.enabled = false`). What is the architectural problem given the multi-team context?
options: External shuffle service should be ENABLED at cluster level. With dynamic allocation reclaiming executors, executor death is expected. Without it, every reclaimed executor's shuffle output becomes unreachable. Risk violates a platform standard.

Should be DISABLED for this workload because the pipeline does not retry on FetchFailedException — disabling avoids unnecessary network overhead at scale. The architectural problem is that the choice is undocumented; document it for the team's runbook.

The setting affects only this pipeline; Risk owns the choice and made an informed engineering decision based on their workload's failure profile. The architectural problem is none — Risk's choice is reasonable.

External shuffle service is incompatible with dynamic allocation; enabling it would prevent dynamic allocation from working. Risk correctly disabled it to enable dynamic allocation. There is no architectural problem here.
fields.correctAnswer: External shuffle service should be ENABLED at cluster level. With dynamic allocation reclaiming executors, executor death is expected. Without it, every reclaimed executor's shuffle output becomes unreachable. Risk violates a platform standard.
fields.rationale: External shuffle service is the architectural prerequisite for dynamic allocation. With dynamic allocation reclaiming executors as workload changes, executor death is EXPECTED — it is by design. Without external shuffle service, every reclaimed executor's shuffle output becomes unreachable; downstream tasks fail with FetchFailedException; cascade compounds (PMSS2.1). Cluster standard: spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true is mandatory for dynamic allocation.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Reverses the standard.

Option C: Treats Risk as sole owner of a platform-wide standard.

Option D: Claims compatibility issue that does not exist.

fields.label: Architectural Problem #3 — Lines 36-50 (PyTorch UDF using ~22GB of native memory per worker). What is the architectural problem given the cluster context?
options: PyTorch UDF is fine for ML inference; 22GB native memory is acceptable for the model size. There is no architectural problem here — the workload is correctly using the right tool for the job.
PyTorch UDF should be replaced with a JVM-native ML library to avoid off-heap cost; the architectural problem is the choice of Python+native-library architecture.
Unbudgeted off-heap on a multi-team cluster. 22g exceeds Risk's overhead of 4g by 5×. On shared nodes this kills other teams' executors via RSS exhaustion. Fix: raise overhead or use cgroups.
PyTorch UDF should be batched to reduce per-row overhead; 22GB is high because each row triggers a model load. Use pandas_udf for batched inference and the memory cost drops by an order of magnitude.
fields.correctAnswer: Unbudgeted off-heap on a multi-team cluster. 22g exceeds Risk's overhead of 4g by 5×. On shared nodes this kills other teams' executors via RSS exhaustion. Fix: raise overhead or use cgroups.
fields.rationale: PMSS4.2 covered this pattern. Python UDF with native ML library consumes off-heap that exceeds the unbudgeted 4g overhead. Risk's RSS exceeds container budget; on shared nodes, this exhausts node-level RSS and kills other teams' executors. Fixes: raise overhead to 24g matching actual need, negotiate contract amendment for total RSS, or use cgroups at the OS level.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Dismisses cross-team impact.

Option B: Treats tool choice as the issue. PyTorch is fine; the missing budget is the issue.

Option D: Picks an optimization that does not address the architectural gap.

fields.label: Architectural Problem #4 — Lines 25-28 (rand()-based salt) + line 31 (FULL OUTER join) + line 16 (AQE enabled with skewJoin). What is the architectural problem?
options: Salt factor is 10, too small for Risk's distribution; the dominant counterparty has 30% market share and salt factor 10 only spreads to 3% per bucket, still 6× normal. Salt factor must be calculated from distribution.
AQE is enabled — for Senior production pipelines, AQE introduces unpredictable plan changes that are hard to debug. Disable AQE for production reliability and predictable performance characteristics.
FULL OUTER itself; FULL OUTER is rarely the right choice for this kind of join. Restructure as LEFT + null-fill or two separate INNER + UNION queries to avoid the FULL OUTER cost entirely.

Chain rand() salt → AQE re-evaluation → FULL OUTER. AQE skew handling does NOT support FULL OUTER. rand() is non-deterministic so AQE produces mismatched salts. Fix: deterministic salt + INNER + null-handling.
fields.correctAnswer: Chain rand() salt → AQE re-evaluation → FULL OUTER. AQE skew handling does NOT support FULL OUTER. rand() is non-deterministic so AQE produces mismatched salts. Fix: deterministic salt + INNER + null-handling.
fields.rationale: Three concerns compound: (1) FULL OUTER not supported by AQE skew handling (PMSI3.2), (2) rand() non-determinism breaks salt across AQE re-evaluations (PMSI4.2), (3) the chain has no fallback. Fix: deterministic salt PLUS restructure to INNER + null-handling. Senior-level skill is recognizing that THREE concerns combine into one architectural fragility.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Identifies real concern (salt factor) but misses the chain.

Option B: Blames AQE; disabling creates more problems.

Option C: Identifies one link but not the chain.

fields.label: Architectural Problem #5 — The pipeline runs successfully on Risk's own SLA but causes cluster-wide incidents on other teams. What is the meta-level architectural lesson?
options: Risk team is at fault for prioritizing their own SLA over cluster citizenship. Recommendation: Risk adopts cross-team awareness during sprint planning and runs impact reviews before deploying changes.
The cluster needs better monitoring; if Risk's team had real-time dashboards showing other teams' impact, they would self-regulate. Recommendation: build cross-team dashboards.
Other teams should be more resilient; their pipelines should tolerate Risk's bursts. Recommendation: other teams add retry logic and increase their own buffer capacity to handle the bursts.

Individual-team correctness does not imply cluster-level correctness. Risk's pipeline is correct in isolation. Cluster incidents emerge from POLICY GAPS at the platform level. Platform encodes constraints in policy.
fields.correctAnswer: Individual-team correctness does not imply cluster-level correctness. Risk's pipeline is correct in isolation. Cluster incidents emerge from POLICY GAPS at the platform level. Platform encodes constraints in policy.
fields.rationale: The meta-architectural lesson of the entire Senior track. Individual-team correctness does NOT imply cluster-level correctness. Cluster-level correctness emerges from POLICY INVARIANTS at the Platform level. Each gap (off-heap budget, RSS quota, dynamic-allocation invariant, external-shuffle-service mandate) allows individual-team-correct behavior to produce cluster-incidents. Encode constraints in policy, not in good-neighbor norms.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Blames individual team norms. Non-scalable.

Option B: Treats monitoring as enforcement. Visibility is necessary but not sufficient.

Option C: Asks other teams to absorb cost. Resilience is valuable but does not fix policy gaps.
